newsitem.title: USA: CIA taught torture methods in 1983 training manual.
newsitem.headline: CIA taught torture methods in 1983 training manual.

text.p: The U.S. Central Intelligence Agency taught torture techniques in the early 1980s, including ways to break a prisoner's will through sensory deprivation and inducing strong fear, a newly declassifed CIA training manual showed.

The guide, "Human Resources Exploitation Training Manual -- 1983," appears to have been designed for training security forces allied with Washington's anti-communist crusade in Central America under former President Ronald Reagan.
The CIA said on Monday that a policy strongly opposing the the use of torture had been written into updates of the training manual between 1984 and early 1985.

A cover sheet inserted by 1985 cautioned students: "The use of force, mental torture, threats, insults or exposure to inhumane treatment of any kind as an aid to interrogation is prohibited by law, both international and domestic; it is neither authorised nor condoned.

"We respect and are committed to internationally recognised human rights standards," Mark Mansfield, a CIA spokesman, said on Monday. "We do not engage in activities that could be construed as support for, encouragement of, or complicity in human rights violations.

"Adherence to human rights principles is not only emphasised in our training but it is intrinsic to all of our activities," added the CIA spokesman, who was long involved in training pro-U.S. security forces abroad.

The 1983 manual was declassified late last week in response to a threatened Freedom of Information Act lawsuit by the Baltimore Sun, which has been investigating alleged torture and murder by a CIA-trained Honduran military unit in the 1980s.

At the same time, the CIA declassified a Vietnam War-era training manual dated July 1963 which, like the 1983 manual, recommended pre-dawn arrests to maximize dread and disorientation, keeping prisoners blindfolded while processing them and taking away their clothes.

Copies of the documents were made available on Monday by the CIA, which declined comment on any link between the Vietnam-era techniques and those detailed in the 1983 manual. Mansfield said he did not know what information about torture techniques, if any, had appeared in pre-1983 editions of the Human Resources Exploitation Training Manual.
The 1983 edition recommended that interrogation chambers be windowless, dark, soundproof and without a toilet.

"The 'questioning' room is the battlefield upon which the 'questioner' and the subject meet," it said. "However, the 'questioner' has the advantage in that he has total control over the subject and his environment."

"Throughout his detention, subject must be convinced that his 'questioner' controls his ultimate destiny, and that his absolute cooperation is essential to survival," the manual said. It defined "subject" as a person thought to have information of value to the service questioning him.

"While we do not stress the use of coercive techniques, we do want to make you aware of them and the proper way to use them," the introduction stated. "The use of most coercive techniques is improper and violates policy," a penciled-in addition to a subsequent version said.
In a chapter titled "Coercive techniques," the 1983 edition discussed heightening stress and anxiety and cited experiments on what it called volunteers placed in "sensory deprivation tanks."

"They were suspended in water and wore black-out masks, which enclosed the entire head and only allowed breathing," the 1983 version said. "They heard only their own breathing and some faint sounds of water from the piping."

"The stress and anxiety become unbearable for most subjects," it added. Mansfield, the CIA spokesman, declined comment on the manual's intended audience. He said the CIA's in-house watchdog, Inspector General Frederick Hitz, was still investigating the agency's alleged role in human-rights abuses in Honduras in the 1980s.
